title: Research
text:
Immune control of heart regeneration. Newborn mammalian hearts can regenerate after injury; adult hearts cannot. My work shows that the PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint pathway maintains the immunosuppressive environment this regenerative window depends on, and asks how T cell populations are recruited and licensed during neonatal cardiac injury.
Self-renewal and ageing of tissue-resident macrophages. During my PhD I characterised a short isoform of Piwil2 required for the self-renewal of murine macrophages, and contributed to work on how alveolar macrophages retain their epigenetic identity through long-term expansion and how microglia mature in the developing brain.

title: About
text:
I am a postdoctoral fellow in the laboratory of Eric Olson at UT Southwestern Medical Center, where I study how the immune system shapes the regenerating heart. Newborn mammalian hearts can rebuild themselves after injury; adult hearts cannot. I work on the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway and the immunosuppressive environment that this regenerative window depends on — research supported since 2025 by an American Heart Association Career Development Award.
I completed my PhD with Michael Sieweke at the Centre d’Immunologie de Marseille-Luminy and the Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine in Berlin, on the molecular mechanisms that allow tissue-resident macrophages to renew themselves, and a Diploma in Molecular Medicine at the University of Freiburg.
Alongside research I chair the webinar committee of the International Society for Regenerative Biology for the Americas, and I speak about the path of a Latin American scientist in STEM.
